name: Maya Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in my first year of law. I live with my parents and grandmother in the flat above our grocery shop on Eastgate Road. I'm at lectures Monday to Wednesday, then I work the till on Thursday evenings and all day Saturday. My father pays me a small wage, but the shop only just breaks even. Sundays are for family and prayer.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: In our area, people sign papers they don't understand. A letter from the council, a landlord's notice, and they panic. I wanted to be the person who can read it and explain it in plain words, in our language and in English. My grandmother says a lawyer in the family is a blessing. No pressure there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. The scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. Big claims come and go. What matters is people, and a person who explains a letter patiently isn't replaced by a program. I'd tell my cousins the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd still be uneasy. The supermarket chain opened two streets away and our takings fell. My wage comes from the shop, and my loan only covers fees. If the shop shrinks, my wage goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the till and keep studying. I'd save what I can, around fifteen pounds a week, and I'd ask the law faculty about the free legal advice clinic, where students sit in with real cases. I'd also pray and keep my family close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slightly anxious, but mostly steady. I've got the habit of getting on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are the worries in the shop, even if nothing changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our takings dropped about a fifth after the supermarket opened. Dad hasn't said it, but I see him checking the till twice. So I'd feel I should find work somewhere else if I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the shop's wages stopped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hard work, family, and good manners solve most things. I'd tell my friends not to wait for handouts, but to do the work in front of them.

say: I'd say a person who explains a letter patiently **isn't replaced** by a program.
I'd tell friends to do the **work** in front of them.
think: The supermarket two streets away already cut our **takings**, and my wage comes from the shop.
My loan covers **fees** only, so any cut to my wage hurts.
do: Keep working the **till** and keep studying.
Ask the law faculty about the free **legal advice clinic**.
feel: Mostly **steady**, with a small knot of worry about the shop.
S0.quote: Our takings dropped about a fifth after the supermarket opened. Dad hasn't said it, but I see him checking the till twice.
fieldNote: Her worry is the **shop**, which pays her wage, not AI.
Values human, patient advice, which matches her reason for studying law.
Traditional outlook shows in hard work, family and no handouts.

steps.text: Keep working the till on Thursdays and Saturdays
Save fifteen pounds a week from my wage
Ask the law faculty about the free legal advice clinic

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. The scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's something to be careful about. I'd say a law is only as good as the person who understands it. I'd tell my cousins that good people will always be needed, but I'm saying that partly to calm myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm uneasy. Reading documents and checking forms is what junior lawyers do, and software does those fast. If firms hire fewer juniors, my years of study might end in a door that's half shut. I try not to think about it at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the course and aim for work with people: housing, immigration, family. I'd keep the shop shifts. I'd probably ask my lecturers what the firms do, but I'd not use the tools myself yet. I'd rather get the thinking in my own head first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, quietly. I don't say it aloud at home because I don't want my parents to worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of legal work do you think software takes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Form filling, contract checking, search. Those I think go first. People who need someone to sit with them and hear their story, those I think remain. That's the part I'm best at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use them if I had to, but late. I like to see a thing proved before I trust it. My grandmother says never buy the first apple at the market.

say: I'd say a law is only as good as the person who **understands** it.
I'd tell cousins good people will always be **needed**.
think: Reading documents is what **junior lawyers** do, and software does that fast.
My years of study might end in a **half-shut door**.
do: Aim for work with **people**: housing, immigration, family.
feel: **Anxious**, quietly, and I don't say it at home.
S1.quote: People who need someone to sit with them and hear their story, those I think remain. That's the part I'm best at.
fieldNote: Draws **a line** between document work and listening to people.
Hides her anxiety from parents, a sign of duty and care.
Delays AI use until proven, consistent with her resistance.

steps.text: Aim my modules and clinic work at housing and family law
Ask lecturers what graduate firms do with software
Delay trying AI tools until my second year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. The scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should pray and plan, and stay calm. In public I'd say it's too fast for anyone. I'd say the government should protect families and small shops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be afraid. The shop might close, my degree might not matter, and Dad has nothing saved beyond the stock. If both his income and mine disappear, we'd depend on my grandmother's small pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at university for now, because leaving the place is hard to undo. I'd work more at the shop to keep it open and cut every spending I can. I'd look at care jobs and hands-on trades because they're last to go. And I'd talk to our community elders about support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel my stomach drop every morning when I see the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the truth, calmly, over dinner. I don't want them to hear it from the news. We'd decide as a family whether I stay at university or help keep the shop alive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay in law?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If we lose the shop, I think we'd stay with my uncle in Dunmore. That's the family way, to share a roof when it's hard.

say: I'd say we should **pray and plan** and stay calm.
I'd say the government should protect **families** and small shops.
think: The shop might **close** and my degree might not matter.
If Dad's income and mine go, we rely on my grandmother's **pension**.
do: Work more hours at the **shop** to keep it open.
feel: **Alarmed**, with a drop in my stomach every morning.
S2.quote: If we lose the shop, I think we'd stay with my uncle in Dunmore. That's the family way, to share a roof when it's hard.
fieldNote: Her fear is for the **shop** and parents, not herself first.
Turns to family and community, in line with traditional values.
Considers hands-on work, a realistic reading of robot timing.

steps.text: Cut every non-essential spend from my wage
Work extra hours at the shop to keep it open
Ask community elders and our faith community fund for support
Plan with family whether to stay with my uncle in Dunmore

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. The scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning we should use well. I'd say families should save, and young people should learn practical things alongside their studies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel more able to cope. By 2031 I'd be twenty-three and just starting work, probably as a trainee. It's right on the edge. But if I'm sensible, I could have some savings and some experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and take every clinic placement I can, so I've got real experience with people. I'd save twenty pounds a week. I'd also help Dad set up an online ordering page for the shop, because many customers have moved to the phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but not frozen. I can see a route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the extra three years change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to move one step at a time. With two years, everything is a rush. With five years you can pray, plan and still sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the shop survive in your view?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the shop going as long as it pays. If we have to close it, I'd want it to be a decision, not a collapse.

say: I'd say five years is a **warning** we should use well.
I'd tell families to **save** and learn practical things.
think: By 2031 I'd be just starting work, **right on the edge**.
If I'm sensible I could have some **savings** and experience.
do: Take every **clinic placement** I can for real experience.
Help Dad set up **online ordering** for the shop.
feel: **Anxious** but not frozen, because I can see a route.
S3.quote: With two years, everything is a rush. With five years you can pray, plan and still sleep.
fieldNote: Time turns **dread** into steps, like a placement and an ordering page.
Wants closing the shop to be a decision, not a collapse.
Faith language shows how she copes.

steps.text: Take every legal clinic placement offered at the faculty
Save twenty pounds a week from my shop wage
Help Dad set up online ordering for the shop
Keep working Thursday and Saturday shifts at the shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. The scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and we shouldn't worry too soon. I'd say work hard and save, and the rest will follow. I'd also tell my younger cousins to study hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel quite hopeful. By twenty-eight I'd be a qualified lawyer, I hope, with a small practice or a job in a community centre. A decade gives me time to prove myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, do the training contract, and put money aside for the family. I'd learn the tools when firms need them, and teach my parents how to use them so they aren't left behind. And I'd still go to the shop on Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slightly anxious, mostly hopeful. The shop worry stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change what you study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want Dad to have retired comfortably and my grandmother to have good care. I'd want the shop sold well, or passed on to a cousin who wants it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you want your family to be placed by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay with law. People will always need someone to explain their rights, and I'd rather be that person.

say: I'd say ten years is long and we shouldn't **worry too soon**.
I'd tell younger cousins to **study hard**.
think: By twenty-eight I could be a **qualified lawyer** in a small practice.
A decade gives me time to **prove myself**.
do: Finish the degree and do the **training contract**.
Teach my parents the **tools** when firms need them.
feel: Mostly **hopeful**, with the shop worry staying.
S4.quote: People will always need someone to explain their rights, and I'd rather be that person.
fieldNote: Hope sits beside the **shop** worry, which doesn't fade with time.
Her plan covers parents and grandmother, not just herself.
Mood stays anxious because the family shop is already struggling.

steps.text: Finish the law degree and complete a training contract
Put aside a fixed amount each month for family care
Learn the tools when my firm needs them and teach my parents
Plan with Dad how the shop is sold or passed on

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. The shop and my degree would both be at risk, and my family has no savings. What would help is support for small shops, student loans that pause when jobs vanish, and elders and communities who talk about it openly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me are quiet but we notice everything. We keep our worries at home. If someone asks properly, we'll tell them.

headlineQuote: People like me are quiet but we notice everything. We keep our worries at home.
portrait: Maya is an eighteen-year-old **law student** who lives above her family's grocery and works the till on Thursdays and Saturdays.
Traditional and faith-minded, she believes hard work, family and patient human advice will always matter.
She has never used an AI tool and wants proof before she trusts one.
The shop's falling takings weigh on her more than any technology, even in the quiet scenario.
She reaches **alarmed** in the two-year case, because the shop and her degree would both be at risk.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario, because both the shop and her degree would be at risk.
whatWouldHelp: **Support** for small shops and loans that pause when jobs vanish.
Elders and communities who **talk openly** about it.
